source.title: Disentangling Polysemantic Channels in Convolutional Neural Networks
source.authors: Robin Hesse; Jonas Fischer; Simone Schaub-Meyer; Stefan Roth

record.file_problem: None apparent; the full paper text, including experimental details, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses superposition as a possible explanation for polysemantic channels and as motivation for its identification heuristic, but does not test the capacity, sparsity, or geometry claims in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper applies a weight-restructuring method to polysemantic CNN channels and reports activation outcomes. Those findings concern channel disentanglement but do not test any listed version's claim about superposition, capacity pressure, causes of polysemanticity, SAE features, or feature dimensionality. Hyperparameter values used to select channels are not recorded as results. Findings cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The paper cites superposition as one possible cause of polysemantic channels and uses sparsity as motivation for its identification heuristic. Its results are only the performance of its own channel-disentangling method in ResNet-50. It does not measure capacity, sparsity, feature geometry, the cause of polysemanticity, LLM features, SAEs or feature dimensionality.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors present a proof-of-concept tool that identifies and disentangles γ-polysemantic channels, with promising results. They note it depends on handpicked hyperparameters and class labels, and does not apply to other forms of polysemanticity.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses attribution-based channel identification and weight restructuring in a pretrained ResNet-50, rather than testing toy networks or measuring superposition geometry.

fits_no_version.finding: After the weight edit, each new channel keeps about 114–125% of the original activation on its own class. It shows −9% or −21% on the other class, and the residual channel is near zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some class-associated polysemantic CNN channels can be explicitly split by pruning preceding-layer weights, guided by attribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Channel #1660's average relevance vectors for 'digital clock' and 'cauliflower' have cosine similarity 0.47.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different concepts in one CNN channel draw on distinct preceding-layer channels.

record.peer_reviewed: 2025 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW), The First Workshop on Mechanistic Interpretability for Vision (MIV)
record.problems: The study is a proof of concept on one pretrained architecture and one dataset, focuses on the penultimate/last convolutional layer, and uses handpicked τ, γ, and p values. The authors state that the formulation is based on class labels and may work better in later layers. No uncertainty estimates or control comparisons are reported for the activation results.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results bearing on the listed claim versions were omitted. Hyperparameter settings and cited findings were not entered as rows.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity transition or feature geometry.
No test of whether capacity limits or feature importance cause polysemantic channels.
Does not establish any cause of polysemanticity. Superposition and a non-privileged basis are only cited as possibilities.
CNN only. No measure of features spread across neurons in LLMs, and no SAE recovery.
No SAE features are evaluated. SAEs are only mentioned in related work.

missing.what: The number of γ-polysemantic channels found in the penultimate layer is never reported; it would indicate how common polysemanticity is. The paper does not give it.

record.verdict_notes: CVPRW 2025 workshop paper on one model (ResNet-50, last convolutional layer). No uncertainty estimates or controls are reported. Superposition appears only as a cited motivation.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy networks, feature overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometries.
Does not test whether limited capacity causes polysemanticity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Does not establish that polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure or identify its cause.
Studies a CNN, not LLM feature distribution or SAE recovery.
Does not evaluate SAE features or their completeness, stability, or canonical status.
Does not test whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.
